Stated Claim / Post Context:
Child mortality falls in all world regions, deforestation in Brazilian Amazon at lowest ever level, protecting Little Tokyo

In today's edition: new data show that child mortality rates have declined in every single global region since 1950, levels of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon have dropped to an all-time low, and a community impact fund is saving LA's historic Little Tokyo district from developers.

Actual Article Body:
Elizabeth Jacyshyn-Owen | Posted on October 19, 2026 |

Photo: E. Diop/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: new data show that child mortality rates have declined in every single global region since 1950, levels of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon have dropped to an all-time low, and a community impact fund is saving LA’s historic Little Tokyo district from developers.

Since 1950, child mortality rates have fallen 27-fold across Europe, 10-fold across Asia, and 5-fold across Africa and Oceania. This means that the average global rate of children who die before their fifth birthday has dropped to 3.5%.

Source: Our World In Data

According to data released by Brazilian space research agency Inpe, deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest has fallen to the lowest ‌level on record in the 12 months through July. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pledged to end deforestation by 2030, after it soared to its highest in 15 years during the administration ​of former President Jair ​Bolsonaro.

Source: Reuters

Evidence suggests that the huge decline in malaria deaths is due to Ghana deploying a combination of all available anti-malarial interventions, from vaccines to preventive meds, mosquito nets and therapeutic drugs.

Source: GAVI

Lead gunshots have long been the largest remaining source of lead pollution in the region, mostly stemming from hunting and shooting. Now, the European Parliament has voted to prohibit its use, including outside of wetlands and sport shooting, with a seven-year transition period. It will be applied across the EU, the EEA, and Northern Ireland.

Source: Bird Life

Thanks to a new law, utilities companies in the US state will need to provide customers with a financial incentive to electrify their homes before offering to replace gas service lines.

Source: Canary Media

In LA’s Little Tokyo district, roughly 100 local residents have pooled their money into a community impact fund in order to purchase and protect legacy buildings. Faced with rising rents due to developers buying historic businesses, many community members feared being priced out of the region and decided to acquire the buildings themselves.

Source: Next City

The rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh, incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees. Putting people and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce means that the factory can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create social and environmental change.

Source: Dezeen

One of Austria’s biggest retail chains has embarked on a pilot rollout of unusual and long-forgotten apples enjoyed in previous centuries, riding an international trend of reviving heirloom fruit and vegetables. The Spar group is working with produce distributor Frutura to return two rare varieties to shops: Ilzer Rosenapfel and Falchs Gulderling, both dating from the 1800s.

Source: The Guardian

When adult spawners make a left turn into the Yakima River each summer, the water can be too hot for them to survive. In order to help these fish, a new project aims to reroute the creek, build a berm to direct cold water spilling into the Yakima and grow more native plants along the banks.

Source: NWPB

In Bolotana, Sardinia, women are driving a trend that could put the village, population 2,266, in the running to be the world’s sixth “blue zone” – geographic areas with unusually high concentrations of centenarians. Sardinia was home to the first such zone, identified more than 25 years ago.

Source: The Guardian
